props.title: Conquest

sections.content: Conquest stands as one of Lucio Fulci's most ambitious yet overlooked fantasy films, blending his signature gore with sword-and-sorcery elements. Coming at the height of the barbarian film craze sparked by Conan the Barbarian (1982), Fulci's take feels more hallucinatory and dreamlike. The film follows a mystical bow-wielding hero and a barbaric warrior fighting against wolf-men and dark forces. Unlike the muscular heroics of The Beastmaster (1982) or the campiness of Deathstalker (1983), Conquest leans into surreal imagery and atmospheric horror.

sections.content: The early 1980s saw an explosion of Italian sword-and-sorcery films trying to capitalize on Conan's success. While most were quick cash-grabs, some directors like Fulci used the genre to explore their artistic sensibilities. Throne of Fire (1983) and The Seven Magnificent Gladiators (1983) stuck closer to formula, but Conquest's ethereal atmosphere and fog-drenched visuals set it apart. Fulci's horror background bleeds through in gory practical effects and unsettling creature designs.

The film's dreamlike quality comes from extensive use of diffusion filters and smoke machines, creating a perpetually misty world that feels removed from reality. This technique would influence later fantasy films like Legend (1985) and Ladyhawke (1985), though those productions had significantly higher budgets. The practical effects, while dated, showcase the creativity of Italian genre cinema during this period. SUBHEAD: Italian Genre Cinema Innovation

sections.content: Conquest represents a unique intersection of Italian horror and fantasy traditions. While contemporaries like Ator the Fighting Eagle (1982) and Thor the Conqueror (1983) copied Conan's formula directly, Fulci incorporated elements from his giallo and zombie films. The result feels more like a dark fairy tale than traditional heroic fantasy, closer in spirit to Excalibur (1981) than typical sword-and-sorcery fare.
